clinicalPearls: A benign, self-limiting cause of acute scrotal swelling in prepubertal boys
There is marked scrotal wall oedema and erythema, often extending to the perineum or groin, but the testis is non-tender
The characteristic feature is impressive swelling and redness with relatively little pain and a normal, mobile testis
The erythema can extend beyond the scrotum, sometimes described as spreading to the inguinal region
It is an important differential of the acute scrotum, where testicular torsion must be excluded
It resolves spontaneously over a few days, and management is reassurance and supportive care
reference.pathophysiology: Idiopathic scrotal oedema is an acute, self-limiting inflammatory oedema of the scrotal wall of uncertain cause, sometimes considered a localised hypersensitivity or angio-oedema-like reaction. The oedema and erythema are confined to the scrotal (and adjacent) skin and subcutaneous tissue, sparing the testis and cord, which is why the testis is non-tender with preserved blood flow. The absence of testicular involvement distinguishes it from torsion and orchitis.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment of the non-tender testis within a swollen scrotum
Doppler ultrasound showing normal or increased testicular blood flow when needed
Assessment for a systemic vasculitis (for example Henoch-Schonlein purpura)
redFlags: Signs of scrotal cellulitis or systemic infection
Evidence of a vasculitis or systemic illness
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and self-limiting, resolving within days without sequelae, though it may recur.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for, or allowing it to mask, testicular torsion
Treating it as cellulitis with unnecessary antibiotics
Overlooking Henoch-Schonlein purpura as a cause of scrotal involvement
Over-investigating a clinically clear benign presentation
management: Exclude testicular torsion first, since this is a benign self-limiting disorder requiring no specific drug therapy
Treat conservatively with reassurance, rest and scrotal support
Give simple analgesia for the comparatively mild pain
Observe for the expected spontaneous resolution over a few days
Assess for an underlying systemic vasculitis such as Henoch-Schonlein purpura if a rash is present
Safety-net regarding possible recurrence and advise re-presentation for worsening pain
